big: Every mutual fund charges a yearly fee, and you never get a bill for it. It comes out of the fund quietly. A small number like 1% sounds like nothing. Over twenty years it is not nothing.

lines: Why should I pay more through you when direct plans are cheaper?
The direct plan is cheaper, and that is a real saving. Let us see how big, and then what the extra cost buys.

alt: Direct and regular plan growth over 10, 20 and 30 years, in lakh rupees
caps: ₹1,00,000 in the same scheme, two plans. Assume the fund earns 12% a year before costs.
A direct plan costs 0.5% a year (assumed), so it grows at 11.5%. The regular plan costs 1.5%, so 10.5%.
After 10 years the gap is small: about ₹3.0 lakh against ₹2.7 lakh.
After 20 years it is about ₹8.8 lakh against ₹7.4 lakh, which is about 16% less.
After 30 years: about ₹26.2 lakh against ₹20.0 lakh. A small yearly gap compounds.

alt: Bars showing a year's return of 12 rupees split into what the investor keeps and the fund's cost
caps: Say the fund earns ₹12 on ₹100 in a year. Costs come out before you see the NAV.
In the direct plan the cost is ₹0.5 (assumed). You keep ₹11.5.
In the regular plan the cost is ₹1.5. You keep ₹10.5.
The extra ₹1 pays the distributor's commission and service. The portfolio is the same.

title: What you pay
stops: TER is already inside the NAV
Direct plan has no distributor commission
TER arrives as a separate bill
Direct and regular hold different shares
h: What you pay, and what you do not
alt: A shield with true and false statements about fund costs
caps: The total expense ratio, or TER, is the yearly fee taken from the fund's assets.
It is already inside the NAV, so there is never a separate bill. A direct plan has no commission.
An exit load is different. It is charged only if you leave within the stated period.

q: A fund has an exit load of 1% for redemptions within one year. Rohan redeems ₹50,000 after 8 months. How much is cut as exit load?
opts: ₹5,000, as the load applies to the whole year
₹500, which is 1% of the amount redeemed
Nothing, as the load stops after six months
₹250, as he stayed more than half the year
why: The load is 1% of the amount redeemed, not 10%. A year's period sets when it applies, not its size.
He leaves inside the one-year period, so 1% of the ₹50,000 redeemed is cut: ₹500.
The period is stated in the scheme document, here one year. Leaving at eight months is still inside it.
The load does not scale with how long he stayed. It applies in full if he leaves within the period.

q: Meena sees two NAVs for one scheme: ₹52.4 for the direct plan and ₹49.0 for the regular. Is the direct plan simply a better fund?
opts: Yes, because its manager picks better shares than the regular plan's manager
No, because the higher NAV shows the direct plan costs more
Yes, because direct plans are allowed to hold riskier shares
No, the portfolio is the same, and the NAV is higher because the cost is lower
why: Both plans have the same manager and the same holdings. The cost is the difference, not the share-picking.
A higher NAV in rupees shows lower cost built up over time here, not a higher charge.
Plans of the same scheme hold the same portfolio, so risk is the same. Only the cost differs.
Same portfolio, lower cost. The saving builds up in the direct plan's NAV over the years.

q: Rohan could buy direct plans himself, but twice in a fall he sold in panic. How should he think about a regular plan's extra cost of about 1% a year?
opts: It buys better performance, since regular plans earn more
It is a penalty for not knowing about direct plans, so he should always switch
A fee for service, worth it only if advice and discipline add more
It is zero in practice, since the NAV already includes it
why: Both plans hold the same portfolio. The regular plan earns less after cost, not more.
It is not a penalty. It pays for advice. For some investors, staying invested through a fall is worth the cost.
A regular plan pays for advice and service. The honest test is whether that is worth the cost to him.
Being inside the NAV does not make it zero. It is a real cost that lowers what he ends up with.

q: ₹1,00,000 grows at 11.5% in a direct plan and 10.5% in a regular plan for 20 years (assumed). About how much less does the regular plan end with?
opts: About ₹1.45 lakh, because a 1% gap compounds year after year
About ₹20,000, as 1% of ₹1,00,000 is ₹1,000 for each of the 20 years
About ₹5 lakh, since the regular plan loses half of the direct plan's gain
About ₹10,000, as a 1% gap is a small amount in all
why: ₹8.82 lakh against ₹7.37 lakh is a gap of about ₹1.45 lakh, or about 16% of the final amount.
That adds ₹1,000 a year without compounding. The gap grows because each year's cost also loses its future growth.
The regular plan loses much less than half. Its final amount is about 84% of the direct plan's.
A 1% gap looks small but compounds. Over 20 years it is far more than a few thousand rupees.

pts: TER is a yearly fee already inside the NAV. An exit load is charged only if you leave early.
A direct plan has no commission, so its TER is lower. The portfolio is the same.
Costs compound like returns. Ask whether the advice is worth what it costs.
